title: Flagstone
summary: Community map of accessibility barriers: report a broken ramp, verify a neighbour's, see it marked fixed. Privacy-first: no ads, no analytics, no trackers.

body:
## The problem

When someone who depends on accessible routes meets a broken ramp or a missing curb cut, reporting it means a municipal form. Describe the problem, submit, wait, hear nothing. Nobody else finds out. There is no way to signal that a barrier is still there, or to confirm that someone fixed it, so one obstacle gets reported by ten people who never learn about each other, and each of them files it from a place they physically go, which is its own disclosure. I met this gap working with the vision loss community. It is the reason for the app.

## The approach

I chose React Native and Expo to force myself to learn cross-platform development while shipping something real. Supabase handled auth and the database so I could focus on the domain problem instead of infrastructure. The pivotal call was implementing [Postgres Row Level Security](https://github.com/Skypie99/AccessMap/tree/main/supabase/migrations) from day one. Barriers are meant to be seen. A shared map is the whole point, but only the person who filed a report can edit its content; status changes like verifying it or marking it fixed are open to the community that shares the map. That wasn't an afterthought; it shaped every feature that followed.

The hardest part wasn't the code. My first designs missed what users actually wanted. They didn't just want to report problems. They wanted to *verify* them, share workarounds, celebrate fixes together. That insight changed everything.

The map was the other hard part. To a screen reader a native map is one opaque view, so Flagstone keeps a parallel, linear list of nearby barriers that opens on its own when a screen reader is detected, and selecting a marker no longer drags focus back to the map. Text follows Dynamic Type up through the accessibility sizes, touch targets hold a 44-point floor, contrast is unit-tested against the WCAG ratio, and when Reduce Motion is on the map camera jumps instead of animating. The app is built and tested against WCAG 2.2 AA, with an accessibility check in CI that fails a pull request below its threshold.

Privacy set the remaining shape. Location is foreground-only: the app declares no background-location entitlement and calls no background-location API, a line the privacy review held when an unrelated fix tried to add the keys. Every submission, anonymous or signed in, runs the same content filter, and any flag or comment can be reported through the abuse-report sheet Apple requires. Photos are capped in size and scrubbed before upload. Accounts can be deleted, with the cascade handled by a tested pipeline. There is no analytics or tracking SDK in the app.

## Where it stands

A map-first mobile app where accessibility barriers are pinned to real city locations. Report one, verify someone else's, and follow up when it gets fixed. The [web build](https://flagstone.skypistudio.com) is browsable today. The iOS app has not shipped. It was submitted to Apple for App Store review on August 31, 2026. Before submission, one early TestFlight build reached a single outside tester. Apple approval and public App Store availability have not been established.

Until that review completes there is no adoption to report, and I would rather say so than imply otherwise. What exists is evidence: a test suite in the thousands, with a dated figure receipted below; a real-device simulator walk that produced 48 findings, 46 of them fixed across four waves and 2 deliberately left open as documented scope calls; and a privacy model whose shape, and the reasons for it, follow.

## My role

**Mine.** Anonymous reporting gets its own write path rather than an `anonymous` flag on the shared one. A flag is a value some later code path can forget to read; a second path cannot be entered by accident. The cost is that two paths drift, and they have. I take that trade because drift shows up in review and a missed flag does not.

The photo scrubber fails closed: if the location data cannot be verified gone, the upload aborts. The alternative was to carry on with the original bytes, which is what an earlier version silently did. The library call it trusted returns nothing at all, so the "stripped" result was always undefined and the untouched buffer went up. For an app where people photograph places they physically go, a false rejection is an annoyance and a false acceptance is a disclosure.

**The agents'.** Effectively all of the implementation, the whole test suite, and most of the diagnosis, across more than 1,900 commits. The simulator walk above was theirs too. They found what it found.

**What I check.** I gate what lands, and I read the failures rather than the summaries. When an audit reports 48 findings, the ones I read first are the ones it closed without a fix, because a process that cannot report a negative is not a process.

## What went wrong

A simulator walk found the flag detail sheet's Report button rendering, looking enabled, taking the tap, and doing nothing. It is the Apple 1.2(b) objectionable-content sheet, and that screen is its only mount point in the whole app, for flags and for comments, so the report mechanism of a product built on things strangers submit was dead in every path, and would have shipped that way.

It had unit tests. They passed. They mounted the sheet on its own, and the defect was in *where the parent mounted it*, which a child's test cannot see by construction. Four comments in the code asserted the broken arrangement was proven practice, each citing another, and the one citation that pointed outside the ring pointed at a screen where that arrangement is correct for a reason that did not apply here.

The structural fix was one line: a closing tag moved from before the pair of sheets to after them. The comments were rewritten as part of the bug, because they were the reason it kept coming back. The repo had already solved this same iOS error twice, and the correct pattern was sitting three lines above the broken one in the same file. The replacement test renders the parent instead of the child, and it was checked the only way that means anything: it fails against the old arrangement.

## Reflection

> Building this reinforced something I already believed: privacy isn't a feature you add later. It's a foundation, especially when the people using your app are sharing vulnerable information about the barriers they face every day.

title: Claude Corp
summary: A governed multi-agent development system I designed and operate: 15 AI roles, a written Constitution, review gates, and autonomy bounded by explicit rules.
status: In active use, on my projects only

heroImage.alt: A minimal orchestration diagram with eight named role nodes around a central hub styled as a Constitution icon, with the Claude Corp wordmark below

heroShot.alt: The Claude Corp front door, with the editorial hero over the agent pipeline diagram and fifteen roles feeding one governed main branch.

cardImage.alt: The Claude Corp front door, with the fifteen-role pipeline under the editorial hero.

shots.alt: The fifteen-role team grid, with each agent card naming its craft from Quinn on product through Morgan on reporting.
shots.caption: Fifteen roles, one governed main branch.

body:
## The problem

Building solo is manageable. Bigger projects are not. When I started coordinating AI agents for more complex work, I hit the same wall every time: without clear decision rights, scope debates never ended. One agent would start building while another assumed we were still in design. No escalation path. No clear lanes. Multi-agent systems need rules, not just good intentions.

## The approach

I designed the operating model before I grew the team. A written Constitution sets the authority order (my intent, then the Constitution, then each role's own file, then its skills), and no agent may amend it. Fifteen roles each own a domain, from product and design through backend, security, QA, accessibility, performance, release, and documentation; a project manager routes decisions to the right lane, and an orchestrator runs the cycles.

The rules that matter most are the ones that remove discretion. Every role works on its own branch, never on main, and merging is mine. Database migrations are files with a rollback, never applied changes. No agent sends anything outside the repository, handles a credential, or acts on a privacy-sensitive change without it reaching me first. Exactly one role may message me; the other fourteen write reports I read on my own schedule. A UI change passes a seven-layer design-compile gate before it counts as done. Work that runs unattended is held to a stricter mode still: at most one reversible change per cycle, no external sends, audit-only by default on the products, and one sentinel file that halts all of it.

There is one exception, and it is deliberately narrow. A single role holds a standing grant to merge and push one project, the Prompt Library, and only when a mechanical gate holds: the full check chain, proof of the built output, a recorded rollback, and nothing on the always-escalate list. The grant is reviewed quarterly and can be revoked; everything else stays a human merge.

## What shipped

A working system rather than a diagram: the Constitution and its runtime overlay, fifteen role files, an orchestrator, a recovery agent that resumes from the last checkpoint and, after three failed attempts, escalates instead of looping, and a QA report trail in every project. Every project on this site was built through it, including this portfolio. The Constitution is a working document, summarized publicly but not published in full, and it changes when the system finds a new failure mode.

## My role

**Mine.** The operating model itself: who decides what, in what order, and what nobody may decide alone. I write the Constitution and the role specifications, write the briefs and acceptance gates a cycle is judged against, review the escalations, resolve conflicts between roles, and hold release and merge authority. The flexible version, letting each agent judge when to escalate, is the one I rejected every time, because judgement is the thing I cannot verify at scale.

**What it does without me.** Before starting, a role scans for another agent's open branch or a fix already shipped, and writes a conflict report instead of duplicating the work. It caught a session that reported pushing a commit to a `main` that was still three commits behind: the claim was confident and wrong, and reconciliation, not trust, is what found it.

**What I check.** The escalations, and the reports of work *not* done. A system that only ever tells me it succeeded is one I have no way to audit. The honest limit: these fences are prompt-level, not sandbox-level, and some of the overhead does not pay for itself.

## Reflection

> The biggest unlock wasn't any individual role: it was realizing that the rules are what make speed possible.

I'd build the governance layer first next time, before writing a single line of application code.

title: Claude Corp Dashboard
summary: The operator console for my agent team: what needs me, what is blocked, how each project is doing. Private in use; a public demo runs on synthetic data only.

body:
## The problem

I'd been coordinating a small team of AI agents, including a project manager, engineers, a designer, and a security reviewer, across several projects at once. The work was getting done, but I had nowhere to actually *see* it. Who's active right now? What decisions are waiting on me? Which blocker is about to slip? It all lived in scattered reports and commit logs. I wanted a cockpit.

## The approach

The dashboard reads the team's own artifacts, the QA reports, decisions, and blockers every role writes, and turns them into an operator's view: an agent feed, a "What Needs You" ledger of the decisions waiting on me, a blocker board, a health grade per project, and velocity over the last week and month. It is a server-rendered Next.js app. In private use it runs against real state, behind a sign-in that admits exactly one GitHub account, mine.

The interesting problem was making any of it public. The real data is sensitive: security findings, private notes, decisions in flight. It can never be published, but a demo nobody can click proves nothing. So there are two builds of one codebase. The public demo runs in a hard-locked demo mode: every data reader short-circuits to a synthetic snapshot before it can touch a real file, every write returns a plausible answer and persists nothing, and a build guard refuses to produce a public build at all unless demo mode is on.

## What shipped

A public demo you can drive. Sign in as a guest, approve or defer a decision, triage a blocker, open the command palette, export the reports view as CSV, switch themes. A Think Tank board that sorts ideas into Do it, Later, and Skip, and a dispatch queue with its relay activity. Fifteen agents in the feed and a health grade per project, all on synthetic data that resets each session. The demo says it is a demo, and it dates the snapshot it was built from, so nobody mistakes the numbers for live operations.

## My role

**Mine.** The seam. The real data here, including security findings, private notes, and decisions in flight, can never be published, but a demo nobody can click proves nothing. I chose three independent layers over one switch. Every data reader short-circuits to a synthetic snapshot before it can reach a real file. The write path is severed, so an approve button returns a plausible answer and persists nothing. And the build itself refuses to produce a deploy until it is told which kind it is, public demo or private real, and refuses a real one outright if the login gate is off.

The alternative was a single demo-mode flag, which is one misconfigured environment variable away from serving my actual findings to the open internet. Three layers means any one of them can fail without leaking.

**The agents'.** All three layers, and the guard that reads the published snapshot back and fails the build if anything in it looks real.

**What I check.** That the layers are genuinely independent: that no two of them fail for the same reason. A defence in depth whose layers share a cause is one layer wearing three coats.

## Reflection

The build taught me that *make it public* and *keep it private* aren't opposites. With the right seam, you can ship a faithful, interactive demo while the sensitive version stays private.

> That separation turned out to be the whole design.

title: Prompt Library
summary: Prompts as reusable assets, not scattered text: organize, search, fill variables, run. Kept in your browser; each run goes straight to Anthropic with your key.
status: Live and evolving · no backend of mine

heroImage.alt: A quiet workspace with a notebook of prompts open beside a laptop, soft natural light from the side

heroShot.alt: The Prompt Library home, with a search bar and category chips over a grid of prompt cards and the featured card leading.

cardImage.alt: The Prompt Library home, with search and category chips over the prompt grid and the featured card leading.

shots.alt: A prompt opened in the library, with variable fields ready to fill above the monospace prompt preview and its copy control.
shots.caption: A prompt opened, with variables to fill and the copy control waiting.

body:
## The problem

A good prompt is a working asset, and mine were being treated as disposable text. The useful ones were scattered across chats, notes, and documents, so finding one meant scrolling, reusing one meant retyping, and improving one meant losing the version before it. I wanted a single place where a prompt could be found in seconds, filled in, run, and refined over time. I set one hard rule for it: no server of mine in the middle.

## The approach

The library lives in the browser. Prompts, favorites, run history, and settings sit in localStorage; there is no account and no backend, and the site is a static export. A prompt can carry variables, so one template fills in differently each time, and a versioned JSON import and export moves a library between machines.

Running a prompt is the one place data leaves the page, and I made that explicit rather than quiet: the browser sends the prompt and the user's own Anthropic API key directly to Anthropic over HTTPS, and nothing passes through anything I operate. The client for that call is hand-built rather than an SDK. It streams the reply by parsing server-sent events itself, sorts failures into typed errors (bad key, rate limit, overloaded, network), counts down live when Anthropic asks for a retry, and lets a run be cancelled mid-stream.

The no-backend rule turned out to be the whole product discipline. There was nowhere to offload a hard decision, so every feature had to be scoped to run on the client and earn its place.

## What shipped

Full-text search across the library, categories and tags, favorites, variable fields, per-prompt run history, and Markdown rendering through a small safe-subset parser instead of raw HTML. A choice of Claude models and a max-token setting. Light, dark, and system themes, and a documented set of keyboard shortcuts for search, running, saving, and switching prompts. Built against WCAG 2.2 AA, with screen-reader announcements on copy and run states and reduced motion honoured. Continuous integration runs typecheck, tests, and lint on every pull request, and GitHub Pages deploys from main. MIT licensed.

## My role

The product idea and the privacy rule that shaped it were mine, along with the call to build the API client by hand so the only network request in the app is one I can read in full, and the wording that describes that request honestly. The agents wrote most of the implementation and the test suite. I use it for my own prompts, so a broken search or a lost run shows up quickly, and I re-read the one network call every time it changes.

## Reflection

> "No server" turned out to be the constraint that kept me honest: every feature had to earn its place with nowhere to offload the hard decisions.

I built this because my own prompts were scattered everywhere. I would keep the constraint and lose the notes app.

title: Ghost Code
summary: A terminal-command trainer and my first real build, made to get fluent in the command line and Claude Code. 56 cards, Arcade and Learn modes, no dependencies.

heroImage.alt: Ghost Code arcade screen with the neon Phantom mascot hovering between four command-token answers, score, and spirit-life HUD in a synthwave cabinet

heroShot.alt: Ghost Code’s title screen, with the arcade cabinet framing the Phantom mascot and Start and Settings glowing below the wordmark.

cardImage.alt: A Ghost Code round mid-chase, with the Phantom in the maze and the command prompt waiting below.

shots.alt: A Ghost Code round in play, with the maze board mid-chase, the code prompt beneath, and score and streak counters keeping pace.
shots.caption: A seeded round in motion: same maze, both themes.

video.alt: A Ghost Code round in motion, with the Phantom on patrol while the code prompt waits below.

body:
## The problem

Command-line fluency does not come from reading about commands. It comes from running them, under a little pressure, until your hands know them. I wanted that fluency in the terminal, in Git, and in Claude Code, and studying a list was not getting me there. So instead of only drilling commands, I built the thing I would practise with: a small game I would actually open again. It was my first real build, and it was meant to be.

## The approach

A prompt appears, four command tokens float in a maze, and you steer the Phantom to the right one. Arcade mode keeps score and takes a spirit for every miss. Learn mode drops the pressure and escalates instead: a retry, then a hint, then the answer. A card counts as mastered after three correct answers, which is a plain local counter rather than anything adaptive, and cards you have not mastered come up more often.

The runtime is one HTML file and a deck file. No framework, no build step, no dependencies, no server. That rule meant every feature cost exactly what it weighed, and it kept the whole game readable in one sitting, which is what a practice project needed to be. The reason to build it, the scope of the deck, and that rule were mine; most of the implementation, the deck validator, and the accessibility audits were the agents', and I played every build.

## What shipped

Fifty-six cards across Claude Code, the macOS terminal, and Git (20, 20, and 16), with a decoy set for each. Keyboard-first play: number keys for the tokens, arrows to move focus, and single keys for the 50/50 lifeline, category, mode, theme, pause, and help. Touch and swipe on phones. Light, dark, and system themes with no flash on load. Progress persists in the browser under one storage key, and nothing is sent anywhere. A GitHub Actions check validates the deck on every push, so a duplicate ID or a decoy that is also the answer cannot land. Built against WCAG 2.2 AA: a live region announces state to screen readers, reduced motion is honoured from the system setting or an in-app toggle, and high-contrast mode is supported.

## Reflection

> The best constraint I gave myself was "zero dependencies."

It kept a first project the right size, and it set the pattern the later ones follow: ship something small and real, then widen it deliberately.
